PRIZE WINNERS AT TORONTO WINTER FAIR
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. The house will be pleased to know that once again an unique distinction has been conferred upon the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar by one of its farm residents, Mr. Albert Kessel, of Valley Centre, who not only won the silver cup for the northwest championship for his grain, but last week was awarded the world championship for his rye at the annual Royal Winter fair in Toronto. I should add that last year, Mr. Kessel won a championship ribbon and first prize for a sheaf of wheat, and a first for oats at the same winter fair.
I might say also that in 1947 Mr. Albert Robbins of Laura, in the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar, won the grand prize for oats and in 1948 a reserve championship for an exhibit of barley at the Royal Winter fair. I am sure all hon. members will join with me in congratulating these Saskatchewan farmers for their successful efforts to improve the products of the Canadian grain growing industry.

Mr. Speaker, according to newspaper reports, one of my constituents won the world championship with his exhibits of oats and barley at the Royal Winter fair. The name of the winner is John T. Eliuk, and in winning this award he became the first such double winner in this fair. Incidentally, Mr. Eliuk was the oat king at the Chicago World fair in 1948. This is not the first time that some of my constituents engaged in farming have obtained world recognition of their ability.
It is a pleasure for me to record the congratulations of this house to Mr. Eliuk upon obtaining such a high distinction as winning this double award. The constituency which I have the honour to represent is noted not only for the richest and biggest oil field in Canada, but also for the type of farmers who are given world recognition for their efforts.

Mr. Speaker, since all these farmers are being mentioned this morning, I believe I should draw the 45781-126
attention of this house to the fact that, although my constituency is one of the richest in minerals in Canada, on Friday Mr. Theo-phile Depatie of Hanmer, Ontario, Sudbury district, was crowned potato king of the world.

I do not
believe it would be fair to let an occasion such as this pass without joining with the other speakers in their congratulatory messages, and I should like to extend congratulations to the district agriculturist from my home town, Mr. E. H. Buckingham, for the part he played in bringing three firsts to Alberta from the Royal Winter fair at Toronto, and in addition, the high singles in those classes. Mr. Buckingham and some of his associates came east with five young people's teams, and in taking home these three firsts has conferred quite an honour upon my fellow citizens and his associates from the province of Alberta.

maintopic: S. S. "NORONIC" DESTRUCTION BY FIRE ON SEPTEMBER 17  JUDG- MENT AND REPORT OF COURT OF INVESTIGATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: S. S. "NORONIC" DESTRUCTION BY FIRE ON SEPTEMBER 17  JUDG- MENT AND REPORT OF COURT OF INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
For the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), I wish to give the house a summary of the report of the court of investigation into the loss of the steamship Noronic by fire on September 17 last.
The Minister of Transport informed the house that under the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act he had appointed the Hon.

5.5.	Noronic
Mr. Justice Kellock, of the Supreme Court of Canada, to act as commissioner and to hold a formal investigation into the loss of that steamship. The commissioner, sitting as a court of investigation, was assisted by Captains H. S. Kane and Robert Mitchell as nautical assessors, and Mr. Neil B. Gebbie as engineer assessor.
Counsel appeared for the Department of Transport; for Canada Steamship Lines Limited, and officers; for the Attorney General of Ontario; for the attorney general of the state of Ohio; and for the Seafarers' International Union. Mr. W. K. Campbell acted as registrar of the court.
The court held hearings in the city of of Toronto on eighteen days in September, October and November, and the final sitting was held at the city of Ottawa on the 21st day of November, 1949.
Many witnesses were called to give evidence, and ample opportunity was given to everyone who had personal knowledge of the circumstances of the disaster to come forward and testify. I think I may say without fear of contradiction that the investigation was searching, impartial and thorough.
The judgment of the court was pronounced this morning in open court as follows:
Court of Investigation
5.5.	Noronic
Monday, the 21st day of November, 1949.
The Honourable Mr. Justice R. L. Kellock, Commissioner
This matter, coming on for hearing before this court at its sittings held at the city of Toronto in the province of Ontario on the 28th, 29th and 30th days of September, the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, and 21st days of October and the 7th day of November, 1949, and judgment having been reserved until this day and the same coming on this day for judgment:
1.	This court doth order and adjudge that the certificate of William Taylor, being passenger inland waters' certificate No. 6703, be and the same is hereby suspended until and including the 21st day of November, 1950.
2.	And this court doth further order and adjudge that the costs of the Department of Transport of this investigation be taxed upon the scale of the Exchequer Court of Canada and be paid by Canada Steamship Lines Limited.
3.	And the court doth not see fit to make any further or other order touching the costs of the said investigation.
R. L. Kellock, Commissioner.
Hugh S. Kane Assessor R. Mitchell
Assessor Neil B. Gebbie Assessor
The commissioner's report, concurred in by the assessors, is embodied in a separate document that has been forwarded to me by the

commissioner in accordance with the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act. I now table a copy of the report, and copies will be available for all members of the house.
The report of the court of investigation is a lengthy document, as befits an investigation of major importance, and should be carefully read by all those who are concerned in preventing a recurrence of such a terrible disaster. I shall not attempt in this statement to review at length the contents of the report, but will endeavour to point out to members of the house some of the more important observations and findings of the court.
In the first part of the report the commissioner reviews the legislation and regulations to which the ship and its owners were subject. He finds that the Noronic was built in 1913 and was constructed without fire-resisting bulkheads. Under the regulations, the ship, as an existing ship, was exempted from compliance with the regulations which came into force in 1939 and which require new ships to be constructed with fire-resisting bulkheads.
The Noronic was equipped with a fire alarm system which was mechanically in good order, with fire-extinguishing equipment consisting of hydrants, hoses, fire extinguishers, pumps, smoke helmets and lamps which had been inspected by the Canadian steamship inspection service on April 23, 1949, and had been approved by the steamship inspector. The commissioner expresses the opinion that the laxity of the inspection in requiring compliance with the regulations could only induce or encourage a similar laxity on the part of the owners and officers of the ship with respect to the vital matter of preparedness for fire.
Pursuant to United States legislation, the provisions of the Canadian regulations were considered by the United States authorities as approximating those in the United States, and a certificate was issued on April 28, 1949, by the inspection office of the United States coastguard admitting the Noronic to the exemptions and benefits provided by United States statutes relating to the inspection of boilers, machinery, hull and equipment. This meant that compliance with Canadian regulations was considered sufficient.
The certificate issued by the Canadian steamship inspection service permitted the ship to carry 600 passengers and 200 crew. At the time of the casualty the ship carried 524 passengers and 171 crew.
There are no regulations applying to Canadian passenger ships on the great lakes with respect to the maintenance of any fire patrol system or as to fire drills for either passengers or crew. However, the commissioner states

that, in his opinion, it is implicit in the regulations relating to fire-extinguishing equipment that there shall be provided by the shipowner men trained to use the required apparatus and so organized that the presence of fire on shipboard may be learned at a sufficiently early stage to make the use of the required apparatus in the hands of such men effective in its control. So far as patrolling for detection of an outbreak of fire is concerned, that is a duty which, it was decided as long ago as 1910 by the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of the Dominion Fish Company v. Isbester, is incumbent upon the shipowner for the protection of sleeping passengers in the case of a ship lying at dock.
In a ship equipped with neither automatic apparatus for detecting an outbreak of fire on board nor an automatic sprinkler system to extinguish it if it did break out, as was the case with the Noronic, an efficient patrol for the detection of fire at the earliest possible moment would appear to be essential. The fire patrol actually employed on the ship was inadequate for the purpose.
The report deals with the organization, or lack of it, of the officers and crew of the ship to meet a situation such as occurred. Only 15 crew members were required to be on the ship at the time of the fire, the remainder being free to go ashore.
After reviewing the evidence of certain witnesses, the commissioner finds that, in his opinion, no one in a responsible position in connection with the ship, either on the ship or ashore, had applied his mind in any serious way to the handling of a situation such as arose on the outbreak of fire on the night in question, although such an eventuality could not be considered otherwise than as one that might occur at any time. Moreover, complete complacency had descended upon both the ship's officers and the management. The fire which actually occurred found officers and crew without any organization designed to deal with such a situation.
The commissioner further states that, in his opinion, it is clear there was no training of the crew with respect to fire or its detection, or what should be done after detection, apart from what might be picked up by attendance at fire drills. The lack of any effective system of patrolling for the purpose of fire detection and the lack of any system by which, when fire was detected, the information of its presence and location could immediately be sent to some central locality, where personnel trained in methods of dealing with fire were available to be sent to the spot immediately, accounts, in the commissioner's opinion, for the loss of life which ensued.
45781-126J
S.S.	Noronic
The commissioner points out that the outbreak of fire on a ship at a time when it has a large number of sleeping passengers on board requires of necessity a pre-arranged plan for arousing and getting them off the ship. The Noronic had no such plan. Any organization which the ship did have was designed to function in other circumstances with a complete crew on board. Accordingly the fire found the ship totally unprepared to deal with the situation. Such efforts as were made to fight the fire were scattered and ineffective, and the heavy loss of life shows clearly the failure of the crew to rouse those sleeping passengers who were unable to escape from the burning ship.
The report states that the evidence established the origin of the fire to have been in a small linen closet located just forward of the women's washroom opening onto the port corridor on "C" deck. The actual cause of the fire was not established, but there was no evidence of the fire having been deliberately set.
The procedure followed in formal investigations of this kind is for the Department of Transport to propound certain questions for the opinion of the court. The report of the commissioner sets out at the end thereof the questions raised and the answers given by the court. Following these questions and answers the commissioner makes some observations on the suspension of the master's certificate and gives reasons for awarding costs. The report concludes with certain recommendations made by the court. I should like to read the more important of the questions and answers which are found on pages 94 to 96 of the report, and which are as follows:
Question 15:	When fire was discovered on the
S.S. Noronic was all possible and proper action taken to save life, to fight, control, localize, and extinguish the fire? If not, in what way and to what extent was the action taken, if any, defective or inadequate?
Answer:	The action taken for the above purposes by the ordinary crew members was no doubt such action as they would be expected to take without direction in such circumstances, no officer of the ship having taken charge of the situation or having attempted to give any general directions, if such was possible at the advanced stage which the fire had reached when the alarm was given.
Question 16: If all possible and proper action was not taken or was not taken soon enough to save life, and fight, control, localize and extinguish the fire, was the master or any other person or persons on the vessel to blame? If so, whom?
Answer:	After the alarm had been given the
only thing it might have been possible to do, which was not done, was for the master to have taken general charge of the situation and directed in an organized way the arousing of passengers, instead of acting himself as an ordinary sailor in such parts of the ship as he could reach.

S.S.	Noronic
Question 17: Were the fire fighting appliances on board the S.S. Noronic adequate? Had they been found satisfactory and in good working order? If so, when and where were they last tested and found satisfactory and in good working order?
Answer:	The fire fighting appliances on board
appear to have been satisfactory and in good working order. The last departmental inspection was on April 23, 1949. Some of the fire hydrants (probably all the outside ones, but none of those inside), and a few of the fire extinguishers had been used since that time.
Question 18: How many of the crew of the S.S. Noronic were lost or injured? How many are missing?
Answer:	There were no losses among the crew.
Question 19:	What was the cause of the loss of
the S.S. Noronic and the cause of the loss of life?
Answer:	The loss of the S.S. Noronic and the
loss of life was due to the failure on the part of the owners and the master to have:
(a)	a continuous patrol of the ship for the purpose of detecting the presence of fire, such patrol as was in existence being limited to approximately fifteen minutes out of every hour;
(b)	in failing to have any organization operative when the ship was in dock with passengers on board by which information as to the outbreak of fire could be promptly dispatched to some point from which men trained in the methods of dealing with fire could be immediately dispatched to the locality;
(c)	in failing to contemplate in any real sense the possibility of fire occurring at a dock, and maintaining only fifteen actually on duty out of a crew of one hundred and seventy-one, the others being free to go ashore and who might be, so far as the master or the officer on duty knew, actually on shore;
(d)	in failing to have any plan for arousing and getting the passengers off the ship in the event of fire while the ship was at dock;
(e)	in failing to train the crew as to the proper steps to be taken on discovery of fire or in fire fighting methods beyond giving them a knowledge of how to operate fire extinguishers and hoses.
Question 20: Was the loss of the S.S. Noronic and the loss of life caused or contributed to by the wrongful act or default of the owners, Canada Steamship Lines, Limited, the master, Captain William Taylor, or any other person or persons?
Answer: The loss of the S.S. Noronic and the loss of life was caused by the wrongful default of the owners and of the master in the respects mentioned in the answers to the last question. While it is true that the owners knew and approved of the organization, or lack of it, designed to deal with the outbreak of fire on the ship while it lay in dock with sleeping passengers on board, the master was not in any way precluded by any instructions from the owners from taking the proper steps himself.
I should like also to read the recommendations which appear at the end of the report:
While anything in the way of recommendation for the future probably arises fairly obviously upon a review of the circumstances covered by this report, it may be of value to gather them together in one place. The following are therefore submitted for consideration in connection with ships carrying more than a minimum of passengers on the major fresh waters:
1.	That the provisions as to the fire resisting bulkheads in regulation XVI of the international convention for the safety of life at sea be made applicable to such ships.

2.	That the provisions of regulation XLIII of the said safety convention, as to the maintenance of an efficient and continuous fire patrol system as well as an automatic fire alarm or fire-detecting system, be made applicable, but such alarm or detecting system should not be restricted to parts of the ship not accessible to the patrol system.
3.	That the provisions of regulation XLIV as to muster lists and the assigning of special duties to different members of the crew in connection with the matters therein mentioned, including:
(a) the muster of passengers; (b) the extinction of fire; (c) warning of passengers; (d) assembling of passengers at muster stations; (e) keeping order in the passages and on the stairways and generally controlling the movements of passengers, be applied. This will necessarily require adequate training of the crew in methods of fire fighting, together with the setting up of and maintenance of and effective organization for dispatching men so trained to the seat of fire at the earliest possible moment.
4.	That such ships be fitted with a sprinkler system protecting all enclosed parts of the vessel.
5.	Muster charts should be prominently displayed in order that each member of the crew may become familiar, not only with his own duties and fire and boat stations, but with those of the crew who are to work with him.
6.	That such ships be fitted with a public address system for directing passengers in an emergency, and that the proper officers be trained as to its use.
7.	That ships at dock should provide adequate and more than a single means of exit to shore.
8.	That passenger ships docking with the intention of remaining for any extended time be required to be connected with the local telephone system so that the aid of the local fire department may be obtained without delay.
I wish to read my colleague's conclusion, as follows:
In conclusion I wish to take this opportunity to thank publicly the commissioner and his assessors for their untiring efforts in this long and arduous investigation, and also all those who assisted the court in the discharge of their duties. The recommendations made by the court will be carefully considered by the department, and I sincerely hope that this investigation, which has been so ably carried out, will be the means of preventing disasters of this kind in the future.

subtopic: RESCUE OPERATION BY H.M.C.S. "HAIDA"

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: RESCUE OPERATION BY H.M.C.S. "HAIDA"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members would wish me to refer here to the successful rescue of eighteen men of the United States air force by the Canadian destroyer Haida. This was the culmination of a search and rescue operation by United States and Canadian forces working together. The job done by Haida and her crew was in line with the splendid record of that fine ship.
I am sure all hon. members will wish to echo the message I sent to the commanding officer: "Well done, Haida; heartiest congratulations."

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RESCUE OPERATION BY H.M.C.S. "HAIDA"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure every hon. member would wish the congratulations of the house as a whole to accompany and to support the message sent by the minister on this occasion.
This is one of the most remarkable examples that can be recalled of a combination of different services of different countries in rescue operations. Not only were there Canadian and United States units in the area, but there was a British unit as well; therefore the units of three services were taking some part in these rescue operations.
Royal Canadian Navy
The effective co-operation so indicated, and the fact that air and navy personnel and all those operating with them from the land stations brought the great developments of science to bear in this incredible rescue, is an indication of what can be accomplished by the association of these great forces.
It is to be noted that the aircraft was down in an unknown area, and could not have been seen from a ship, except probably by chance. Air and naval forces combined in a heroic manner, but the ultimate heroism undoubtedly was that of the men in the small whalers from the Haida, and later from the Magnificent, who took a gallant part in making the rescue and transferring medical personnel.
We admire the gallantry of our men and the skill displayed by all who took part in this operation.

subtopic: CHURCHILL WEATHER
speechtext: Prior to September, 1948, five-minute network weather forecasts were broadcast for prairie region on midwest network four times daily, but distribution was limited largely to CBK, Watrous, Saskatchewan, as most of the other stations did not carry these reports. Following inauguration of CBW, Carman, Manitoba, and CBX, Lacombe, Alberta, in September, 1948, prairie reports were broken down on a provincial basis, each CBC transmitter giving full coverage of respective provinces plus adjacent weather areas in neighbouring province to provide overlapping service to listeners. Churchill weather region has been reported continuously six times daily on CBW, Carman, Manitoba, since September, 1948. In addition, CBK, Watrous, Saskatchewan includes adjacent Reindeer and Flin Flon weather regions in Saskatchewan forecasts now given five times daily.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
Under standing order 116 this motion cannot be moved at this time without the unanimous consent of the house. The house knows that there are two applications for incorporation of companies among the private bills listed on the order paper. These applications have to be dealt with by parliament under the legislation adopted last year with reference to pipe lines. It is immaterial to the government and a matter of indifference whether these applications are adopted or not, but it does seem that there

should be an opportunity for the house to express its views on the question whether the charters should be granted.
The bills in question have been before the house on four occasions during the hour reserved for private bills, and on each of those occasions the time allotted proved to be too short to permit of an expression of opinion by the house. It would perhaps be the feeling of hon. members that there should be an opportunity to permit of a decision being made by the house.
As this motion refers to private bills, under standing order 116 it would have to go to the committee on standing orders unless there was unanimous consent to have it dealt with at once. If there is any objection to its being dealt with at once, I would move that the motion be referred to the committee on standing orders.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has anticipated the point of order I was going to raise, but I feel that I should raise a parallel point of order with respect to his suggestion that this motion be referred to the committee on standing orders. Standing order 116 reads:
Except in cases of urgent and pressing necessity, no motion for the suspension or modification of any standing order applying to private bills or petitions for private bills shall be entertained by the house until after reference is made to the committee on standing orders or to one of the committees charged with the consideration of private bills, and a report made thereon by one of such committees.
As the Prime Minister has pointed out, this makes it quite clear that the motion standing in his name on the order paper today cannot be moved in the house unless there is unanimous consent. If the motion is out of order in its present form under standing order 116, then I do not see how the Prime Minister can, without giving notice, propose his motion to refer the matter to the standing orders committee. It seems to me that the course the Prime Minister should follow is to withdraw this motion and give forty-eight hours' notice of a motion to refer the matter to the standing orders committee. That is the procedure that is followed every year toward the end of the session with respect to divorce bills that have come in late. It was the procedure followed in April of this year with respect to some of the pipe lines bills.
I shall refer only to the point of order, and will not transgress the rules of the house by going into the merits of the question; but it does seem to me that the rules are quite clear, first, that this motion cannot be put because it abrogates standing order 116, and, second, that the Prime Minister is now making a 45781-127
Business of the House
motion to refer a matter to the standing orders committee without having given the required notice of such a proposal.
A ruling upon this point will be found in Beauchesne's third edition, beginning at page 685. Incidentally there is an interesting extract from what Sir Richard Cartwright said in connection with that ruling, as found on page 688, when he pointed out the iniquity of asking for special consideration for any particular private bill.
My only point at this moment is that the rules of the house should certainly be followed, particularly with regard to private bills. As a matter of fact, citation 9 in Beauchesne's third edition makes a particular point of that by saying:
The practice is more stringent with regard to private bills.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I for one do not feel that unanimous consent should be given to abrogating standing order 116, and likewise I contend that the proposed motion of the Prime Minister is one which calls for forty-eight hours' notice.

There is one point I wish particularly to make, because it may facilitate the proceedings. We should discuss the motion without any suggestion that it is other than it really is. Its purpose is to make a special provision with respect to two private bills that have been under consideration, having to do with the pipe lines legislation introduced earlier this year.
This motion raises an important question which goes beyond the point of its regularity or the suggestion that it might be referred to the standing committee on standing orders. Ordinarily, as has already been pointed out, it should not be introduced without notice. There is no occasion for any uncertainty about what is contemplated, because at page 1805 of Hansard of November 15, 1949, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) indicated that the government is interested in seeing that these bills come forward under conditions which are not made to apply tc other business introduced by private members.
In his introductory remarks on the motion the Prime Minister said frankly that there are two applications for private bills in connection with pipe lines, and by referring

Business of the House
thereto he indicated that the purpose of the motion relates to these two private bills. He said that the government had no special interest in these bills, but felt there should be an opportunity for the members of the house to pass judgment on them, and that the members should not be deprived of that opportunity by the limitation provided by standing order 15.

Except in cases of urgent and pressing necessity, no motion for the suspension or modification of any standing order applying to private bills or petitions for private bills shall be entertained by the house-

standing orders, and that standing order 116 does not apply to procedure in the house as set forth in standing order 15. I should like the house to take that matter into consideration.

Mr. Speaker, there is a good deal more to this motion than a simple suspension of the provisions of a standing order. In view of the introductory remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), it seems to me it is impossible for us to forget in any stage of the discussion that his motion is directed particularly to two pipe line bills. This being so, I suggest it is essential that we carefully examine exactly what it is we are being asked to do.
There are before the house two pipe line bills which have been presented by private members in the ordinary way. They carry out a detail of the broad measure passed earlier this year providing for the incorporation of pipe line companies. I confess at the time the bill creating the general provisions was before the house I had not contemplated the possibility that hon. members would be called upon to pass judgment on a private bill without any knowledge as to what the effect of it would be. If I had been aware that the provision as to incorporation carried with it the suggestion that the house should pass upon bills in connection with which we are given no details upon which to base our judgment, certainly I would have objected to the particular section of the general bill at

Business of the House
that time, and to any of the related sections, and would have placed before the house the objections I now have.
I suggest this should be in our mind when we are asked to support the motion because its only purpose is to provide a special opportunity to deal in a special way with these two bills. Nothing has been put before the house to show why they should be placed in such a peculiarly favoured position. The merits or purposes of the bills are not so much in issue now as the procedure that we are asked to support. We are told that the limitation of the opportunity for debate on private bills should not, under our democratic system, deprive hon. members of the opportunity to exercise their right to say whether or not such measures should become law. That argument sounds like one in support of the principles of democracy that we are seeking to preserve; but if the principle is sound, why does it not apply with equal or greater force to public bills and orders that are on the order paper?
After all, public bills and orders deal with equally important matters. They are not related to some limited personal or corporate interest. Public bills and orders relate to the broad welfare of the people. Under our democratic procedure it is not incumbent upon every member of the house to indicate his support of the views set forth in resolutions or bills to be found in the list of public bills and orders; nevertheless they relate to matters which are just as important as or more important to the people of Canada than the two pipe line measures. If the principle is sound that limitation of debate should not be so imposed as to restrict the opportunity of members to exercise their democratic right to express their opinion on any matter properly before the house, then I submit that the argument applies with greater force to public bills and orders than it does to private bills which can be transferred to government business and supported as government bills if that is in fact the desire of the government.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at one o'clock, I had referred to the fact that this motion is one which places before the house the responsibility for determining whether the ordinary procedure should be departed from in relation to two particular bills. While the house naturally accepts without question the ruling that the principle involved in the bills concerned is not debatable, the nature of the bills which call for this motion is a subject for consideration at this time.
The point that I had made just before one o'clock was that the government, in its explanation, suggests that it has no particular concern about the subject matter of these bills, but that it does not think the limitation of time provided by a standing order should make it possible for the members to be deprived of an opportunity of voting on these two particular bills. I had pointed out that the same argument applies to public bills and orders. If it is sound in this case to ask the house to change the standing order to extend the time for this particular purpose, it would be equally proper to make sure the members have an opportunity of expressing their judgment on matters placed before this house by hon. members. I went further, and suggested that if this is to be accepted as a precedent, and all motions of this kind do become precedents by acceptance, then we should consider the fact that public bills and orders are on a higher plane than private bills.
Public bills and orders are introduced on the responsibility of members who have been elected by their representatives to share, not only on behalf of their constituents but collectively on behalf of all the people of Canada, the responsibility of government in Canada. In the other case, the procedure is one under which individuals or corporations present petitions and then have their bills sponsored in the house by those who quite often show little attachment to the subject matter of the bill. Having complied with the provisions by way of petition, the bill then comes forward with someone's name attached to it without much suggestion that that individual is seriously identified with the subject matter of the bill. The fact that that is so is evident in this case, because it has already been explained that one hon. member of this house was to have had his name attached to the bill originally, but that was withdrawn and someone else was found who was willing to have his name attached to it.

I suggest therefore, Mr. Speaker, that a decision to vary the regular procedure for this particular purpose should not be contemplated unless the basic argument that the members should have a democratic right to express their opinion in regard to it and register their position should also apply with equal force to public bills and orders. I suggest that it does create a precedent which should be examined carefully. No other reason has been put before us by the Prime Minister in support of this motion. If action were taken by this parliament to extend the time of debate for a purpose so undefined, I would suggest that it would be equally appropriate to present a similar motion at any time to diminish the time of debate. If that is so, then the standing orders would cease to have very much effect in controlling the debates and the orderly business of the house.
While the Prime Minister pointed out that the subject matter of the bills is not one of direct concern to the government and that the point which is really being raised is the democratic right of the members to express their position on the bills themselves, I would point out that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in his remarks on November 15 certainly left the impression that he, at any rate, was greatly concerned about whether or not a decision was made on these bills. On that occasion he made the statement that a good many uninformed assertions have been made in the house about these bills. It is not to be wondered at, Mr. Speaker, that uninformed statements might be made since we have no information other than the fact that in two cases solicitors are applying for incorporation; that no route is outlined and that, having received incorporation, these companies will attempt to obtain the requisite authority afterwards.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that I am not discussing the principle of the bills but the principle with which we are confronted, when I point out that these bills are different from bills incorporating railways, another type of common carrier. It is true that what is carried is different but the railways, as common carriers, present their petitions in a similar manner. But in every case in which a railway presents a petition for a similar incorporation, they must state exactly where they intend to go.

I think perhaps it would be just as well if I were to refresh the memory of the house with regard to what the minister said on that occasion, since he questions my statement. At the bottom of page 1805 of Hansard he is reported to have said:
I said that the first requirement under the Pipe Lines Act is that the company shall be incorporated by act of this parliament. I pointed out that the company must next acquire the gas sufficient to justify a pipe line, by contract with producing companies or by other means. I then pointed out that the company must obtain an export licence from the province of Alberta which, through its own legislation, has retained jurisdiction over the export of gas from that province. I then pointed out that the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada must be satisfied with the route of the pipe line and satisfied with all particulars regarding the construction of the pipe line.
I stated that one requirement of the board of transport commissioners would be the assurance that an export licence under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act would be forthcoming. That act is administered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and its function is to make sure that electricity or fluids are not exported until the present and future requirements of Canada are satisfied. It is therefore seen that there are ample safeguards for the public interest of Canada.
A good deal has been said about possible routes of the pipe line. A good many uninformed assertions have been made in the house in that regard. I know nothing about the pipe line company which is asking for incorporation under this bill;-
That is, Prairie Transmission Lines Limited.
-but I do know something about the interests that are asking for incorporation under another bill now before the house. I know that that company has surveyed five routes from Alberta to the Pacific coast, and that one of them at least is an all-Canadian route. There is no difference whatever between my opinion and opinions expressed here that Vancouver must not be on the end of

the pipe line. Vancouver must be served before any considerable service is taken off for supply to the United States. Under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act that requirement would have to be complied with before any export permit will be given by the department of which I am the minister.
However, I do think that these acts should be studied, and studied very carefully. I should like to know much more about the incorporation asked for in the bill about which I am speaking than I know at the present time. But the place to obtain that information is in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines to which this bill will be referred, and before which the sponsors of the bill will appear to make their case for incorporation.
I will say this, however, that since incorporation by act of parliament is a requirement of the Pipe Lines Act, that incorporation should not be refused on trivial grounds. It seems obvious to me that if a responsible group of men, be they Canadians or Americans, properly financed and having the proper background of experience, apply to this parliament for incorporation, they are entitled to incorporate.
I should like also to say a word about what seems obviously to be a filibuster in connection with these bills. The government will not permit any small number of members to prevent this house as a whole from voting on a private bill. If these bills continue to be talked out in the limited time permitted for private bills, the government will ask the house to suspend the rules and provide whatever time is required to finish the discussion and to obtain a vote on such bills.
Then I believe in some part of it there is a reference to one of the parties in this house; and the closing words of the minister are:
Therefore, I hope that these pipe line bills will be examined and if they are properly sponsored I hope that this house will grant the incorporations.
I would have thought that was a fairly complete summary and a fairly definite statement that the minister thought that the bills should be adopted. That is what the words seemed to imply; and it is the right of the minister to say so. But what we are being asked to do here is to abdicate our responsibilities and to follow this particular course. The word "filibuster" and the word "obstruction" have both been used to describe tactics. I happened to notice that at the time this bill came up for debate on the last occasion only four or five members of the house had spoken on it. That seems to be a fairly limited number to describe as a filibuster. There is something much more than that involved here. The right of hon. members to express their opinions on matters of this kind is not one that should be denied by the mere majority of hon. members, following the lead of the government in regard to bills that are presumably private bills and not bills put forward with the responsibility of the government.
We should not be asked to take the position that because the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has informed us that a number of other agencies must exercise their judgment we should exercise none. Yet,

that is precisely the position in which we are being placed by the way these bills come before us in this house. The procedure is one that does not invite the co-operation of the minority members of the house. As has been pointed out on a number of occasions, it is not only a legitimate practice, it is in many instances a very necessary practice, for hon. members to avail themselves of the rights they have to prevent what they regard to be an improper course. Every hon. member who thinks that an improper course is being followed has a duty to exercise whatever rights he has under the rules to prevent that course reaching its improper result.
Call the discussion which has taken place a filibuster; call it obstruction; call it what you will, it has only been the presentation of things by individual members of the house -and I might point out individual members of both sides of the house-as the reasons why they do not think that the bill should be dealt with in this particular way. But I was struck very forcibly by the fact that a number of hon. members on both sides of the house indicated that they were quite prepared to support bills which gave, them the information that they thought was essential for them to assume their actual responsibility. I do not think it is for the hon. members to abdicate their responsibilities.
I suggested this morning that if the right is not included, if we are not to be given information fully, another course would be to bring in an amendment to the pipe-line bills, which should be brought in this session, treating the incorporation of the companies merely as a formal procedure, imposing no responsibilities on those who grant the charter except to see that the form is complied with. If that were done I am sure hon. members would support such an amendment; but, Mr. Speaker, one of the issues before us in this particular motion is whether parliament, when it passes on something, is going to insist that it have the facts upon which it can base a judgment. I for one do not believe that any hon. member of this house should be asked to pass judgment on something in regard to which he has no essential information. It is for that reason and the other reasons I have explained that I shall oppose this motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that by this time we are all aware of the fact that this is a most unusual motion. In addition to the motion being unusual it is quite clear that the reason it is taking time, the reason it is contentious, is to be found in the attitude of
Business of the House
of Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), when he spoke a week ago tomorrow night. I do not think anyone would deny the fact that this house has shown itself on many occasions prepared to co-operate with any reasonable suggestion. I am satisfied that if the government had gone about this thing in a reasonable way we might not be taking up the time that this house is having to spend today on this matter; but you cannot threaten a democratic parliament and not have it cost at least time.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that some of us have wondered who helped the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) draft this motion. It is so unusual I wonder whether it came from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. As I say, I have gone back and looked over the records of the past. In the noon hour there was not time to go through everything that has happened since 1867 down to the present time; but I went to the library and pulled out the Journals, and in some instances Hansard, of certain years of the past, some of them deliberately but many of them at random. For example, I pulled out both the Journals and Hansard tor the year 1872, the year the bill went through respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, a private bill, a very important bill in the life of this country, introduced by a private member by the name of Mr. Grant. I pulled out volume after volume across the years, and looked at standing orders that were suspended. In no case did I find a standing order suspended for the purpose of giving more than the allotted time to private bills. Just in case it might have happened in a certain period in the life of parliament I took the years from 1930 to 1935 and pulled out every year, and looked at every standing order that was suspended during that regime, and not once was a standing order suspended for the purpose of giving extra time to the consideration of a private bill.
I may say that standing orders have been suspended frequently, shall I say, in every session of parliament. The kinds that are usually suspended are the standing orders that have to do with the petitions being filed in time. But I repeat, never has there been an instance, so far as I could find out, where extra time has been taken away from public business and given to private bills.
I read with interest over the week end some of the debates respecting these very rules regarding private bills when they were passed back in 1867 and revised in the early seventies. The whole spirit of those debates was that private bills must be subjected to a special stringency not applied to public bills and government measures. Therefore, I

Business of the House
emphasize the fact that this is a most unusual precedent that the Prime Minister is bringing before parliament at the present time.
There was an occasion in 1895 when an attempt was made to suspend a certain standing order having to do with private bills, although it was not the particular standing order that we have been considering today. During the course of the discussion on that matter none other than Sir Richard Cartwright, who was quite an outstanding Liberal, had something pretty forceful to say. This was on July 5, 1895. Sir Richard Cartwright said:
There are a number of important bills that we have no chance of touching. The government do not propose to suspend the rules of the house and let them have a chance, but in favour of this bill they propose to suspend all the rules of this house, because by accepting this motion, you practically decree that our standing orders are of no consequence whatever, that every standing order of this house may be abrogated without notice, a proposition that seems to me to be a monstrous one.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that that position taken by Sir Richard Cartwright, namely, that the house should oppose any effort on the part of the government to give extra time to private bills, at the expense of private members' public bills and at the expense of government legislation, is a monstrous proposition that should not be tolerated in this house.
I call as another witness another Liberal, the present Prime Minister, who had something to say on a similar matter in this house on October 28 of this year. On that occasion, bearing in mind we had not concluded the debate on a motion before the house having to do with federal aid to education, I moved an amendment to a motion the Prime Minister presented to the house, and in my amendment I asked that we have one more private members' Wednesday, and that the order of business be arranged so that on that one more Wednesday we might continue to discuss, not private bills, but a private member's resolution relating to a matter of public policy-and a very important matter.
What did the Prime Minister have to say? He said:
I do not think it would be a good precedent- Note that, "good precedent"-
-to have the house decide that any one of these academic resolutions submitted by hon. members should have precedence over the other. The rights of each member are equal, and when there Is an opportunity for those rights to be exercised, it seems to me that they should be exercised according to the provisions of the standing orders.
And then later he said:
There should not be a day especially set aside for the continuation of the debate on the resolution of the member for Saskatoon.

Well, when we have now the same Prime Minister, who would not agree to this house taking further time to discuss a matter of public policy, moving a motion which gives special consideration to two private bills, I am wondering who these people are who get this special consideration.
That led me to look up the names of some of those who are behind these bills. I find that in one case one of the promoters is none other than a certain John Black Aird. I would like to know if he is the same John Aird who appeared before the committee investigating the Beauharnois power project on July 17, 1931, and was asked a long string of questions, just one or two of which I would like to quote.
Q. Is it fair to sum up your recollection of your conversation with Mr. Sweezey this way: You met him and asked him how he was getting along: He said he was having a bit of trouble and you said, "Perhaps I can help you out, but I want 50 cents a horse-power or $125,000 if you get the contract?"
A. That was the first conversation; yes.

But there is no doubt that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was here for the proceedings to which I referred. Then when we came back after the Easter recess we were informed on the Monday night that parliament would be prorogued or dissolved on Saturday of that week. With respect to the suspension of standing orders, look up the Journals for that week and you will find that it was done with respect to a great many of those bills, except that no extra time was allowed. But other standing orders were set aside one after the other, at the request of the government, to facilitate getting those incorporating bills through.
The whole picture during that period of time at the end of April, just before the election at that, was to me an indecent one, confronted as we were with this desire of the government to get these pipe line companies incorporated.
Now, after all that indecency we had last April, we have this instance of a little delay in the house with respect to the second reading of these bills, at which time the Minister of Trade and Commerce gets up and accuses the house of filibustering. Along with that he accuses this party of being responsible for that filibustering, whereas up to that time only one member of this party, the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones), had spoken to those bills, and very briefly at that.
After that charge by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that a filibuster was being carried out we receive this threat that unless the house passes these bills there will be this special kind of motion brought in. Well, apparently the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave the house one more chance on Friday night to see whether the bills would go through. They did not go through, so that now we have this motion.
But I ask hon. members to note that no matter how much the government may try to put forward the niceties of the situation and say that they are still private members' bills, the house should note that the Minister
Business of the House
of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister have brought in this motion to facilitate getting these bills through-and that, by the way, in spite of this quotation from Bourinot -and I am not speaking to a point of order, Mr. Speaker, but just as a matter of argument, where he says at page 581:
It is a recognized principle in the Canadian, as in the English parliament, that ministers of the crown should not initiate or promote private bill legislation. But ministers sit on private bill committees in the Canadian commons-
And notice this-
-and carefully scrutinize all private and local legislation with a view to guarding the public interest.
And there is a footnote which says:
In England, the occupants of the treasury bench are exempt from serving on private bill committees.
I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister will tell us that they did not initiate these private bills, and that in the strict sense they are not promoting them. But they certainly are the two persons in this House of Commons who are facilitating getting these bills through.
In the light of these precedents and in the light of the practice that ministers of the crown stay away from these private bills and especially company incorporations where such huge sums of money are involved, they have made a serious breach-both of them- in what they are doing at the present time.
I intend to bring my remarks to a close.

speechtext: I am glad to note that my amendment is accepted even before hon. members hear its terms. As has already been pointed out, under standing order 15 an hour is set aside on Tuesday nights for private and public bills, the former having precedence.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSIDERATION OF PRIVATE BILLS

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSIDERATION OF PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) does know that. I wish the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) knew it, and I wish the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) knew it. I wish whoever drafted this motion had known it and recognized that fact.
The motion before us proposes to extend the time allotted for the consideration of private bills. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has pointed out, if there is to be any fairness in a proposal to change the rules,

Business of the House
such rules should be changed on the basis of equality as between private and public bills. If the time is going to be extended, let it be extended, not just for private bills but for public bills also. As a matter of fact, if there is to be any distinction it ought to be the other way around: there ought to be allowed extra time for public bills rather than extra time for private bills. So if this motion is before us, despite my objection to it this morning, I feel that some attempt should be made to make it a proper motion. For that purpose I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis):
That the motion be amended by inserting therein between the word "private" and the word "bills," at each of the three places in the said motion where the phrase "private bills" appears, the words "and public," so that in each case the phrase "private bills" will read "private and public bills."
May I point out, before someone else does, that if this amendment were to carry and if it were ordered that tomorrow evening the hour for private and public bills shall be extended to the three-hour period, if the debate on the private bills consumed the whole of the three-hour period then of course we would not get to public bills. But I admit that that is the way the standing order now stands, that private bills always have precedence over public bills in the hour allotted. However, because of the way the Prime Minister has worded his motion, if we have not finished with private bills at nine o'clock tomorrow night we can continue for the rest of the evening, but with a proviso attached. Thus, if we finish private bills at ten o'clock, do we then take public bills? No, we go on with the business that was in hand at six o'clock.
I submit that somewhere in this picture there should be some element of fairness. My contention is that the attitude shown toward these pipe line bills through the whole piece has been one where the government, led by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, has gone just a little bit too far. I submit that this disregard of the primary importance of government legislation and of public bills over private bills has been carried just a little bit too far.
The whole business is amazing to all of us. What we are witnessing in this house in connection with this private bill matter, what we are witnessing in the action of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce in attempting to facilitate the passing of these bills, is indeed as bad as we are saying it is; in fact it is a whole lot worse. I have been startled at the number of things

which have been done during this session which are contrary to hundreds of years of British parliamentary practice.
True, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been mixed up in most of them, but that is no reason why the government should continue to make this kind of mistake. I hope the amendment I have moved will be accepted. Even if it is, it will not be satisfactory, but if we are going to change standing order 15 with respect to Tuesday evening at least it will be changed so that the additional time provided will permit consideration, not just of private bills but of private and public bills as provided for by the standing order itself.

Before reading the amendment may I say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that I noted his remark when he reminded me that he did not approve of my ruling this morning. Standing order 15 provides for the order of business as follows:
Monday (private members' day).
Private bills
That standing order is regularly suspended. I think it has been suspended in every session which I have attended without any reference to the committee on standing orders.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSIDERATION OF PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the proposed motion is accepted by the house the result will be that tomorrow evening private bills will be considered after nine o'clock rather than being restricted to the hour between eight and nine. I assume that if the government does not achieve its purpose of having these two bills put through tomorrow night it will take further steps to see that they are passed before the end of the session. As has been mentioned by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the effect of this move is to put aside government business, the business of the country, in order to allow these private bills to go through.
In fact the government is forcing these two private bills to a vote at a time when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is professing complete indifference as to whether they are passed. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is not quite so naive. He has expressed everything but indifference with regard to the bills. The effect of the government's action will be to benefit two groups of individuals who are applying for

incorporation of two natural gas pipe line companies, one company to be known as the Alberta Natural Gas Company and the other as Prairie Transmission Lines Limited.
Not only will the effect be to benefit these individuals who have applied for charters- we all know that they are applying on behalf of undisclosed principals-but I understand that one incorporation is in effect being sought by a company known as Northwest Natural Gas Company which is described in the Financial Times of November 18 as a United States corporation which plans to pipe Alberta natural gas south into the states of Washington and Oregon with side lines to southern British Columbia cities, such as Vancouver.
Has the government actually the gall to pick and choose among private bills and to say, "We like this private bill and we want it to go through"? That is what they are doing here. They are picking two private bills and attempting to force them through the house, or in any event to force them to a vote. After the stand taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), everyone knows that it will be a most independent-minded Liberal, such as the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), who will stand up and vote against the bills. If this is to be the course followed by the government, then why not change the rules? If they are going to force these measures through, then let them be honest about it, change the rules, and provide that these things can be done legally.
May I point out that the government is attempting to force these bills through despite the fact that there is a most important issue at stake.

majority is so large they feel they do not need to care what the people think about what members on the opposition side of the House think. If the Prime Minister is not promoting these bills, he is certainly facilitating their passage through this house.

speechtext: Any measure that comes into this house according to the rules of the house, that is the point I wish to make. The bills which come before this house are of three types. There are government bills which the government usually carries without much difficulty. There are public bills which are put forward by private members of all parties. If it so affects the interests of the country that those individuals must come here for a charter, surely it does not automatically follow that they must receive a charter merely upon presentation of a bill.

If that is not the principle of parliamentary procedure, then I do not know what parliamentary procedure really is. Private bills are in a particular category. We have adopted a system wholly vicious, a system by which members of the house are expected. not merely to introduce and take the first steps in connection with the passage of private bills, but also to become their advocates and active promoters, and the position which we see is assumed with regard to such bills is one which is quite inconsistent with the true position of members of parliament called upon to pass judgment on them.
If we are to be free members of parliament, we cannot put ourselves in the position where
Business of the House
we are supporting private interests outside this house. There is nothing further I wish to say on this subject. As I said, I believe a debate should be allowed on the merit of the bills; for how can anyone say whether the rules should be suspended if there is not some particular reason for doing so? The motion, as it is based on part 4 of standing order 15, should also apply to public bills unless the government takes the position that these private bills are more important than the half dozen public bills that are on the order paper. It seems to me that it would be infinitely better if we had been able to discuss the matter on its merits; and I am afraid that many people will feel that that is not being done at the present time. I had a phrase running through my mind, and I have sent out to find out a little bit more about it. There is an old phrase, which will be familiar to the lawyers, and which was in use at the time when the strict rules of law which had been so rigid and unyielding were tempered by rules of equity. It became a saying that equity was determined according to the length of the foot of the chancellor. I will read you a short explanation:
Equity is according to the conscience of him that is chancellor, and as that is larger or narrower, so is equity . . . one chancellor has a long foot, another a short foot, a third an indifferent foot. Tis the same thing in the chancellor's conscience.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if this motion goes through, we are going to deter-

mine this matter not on the merits of the case but really, as has been suggested, according to the shortness of the temper of the Minister of Trade and Commerce; and I think that would be a most unfortunate thing.

Some of us were asking for the privilege of speaking for two or three hours on the subject of education; but we were assured that so much government business was before the house that we could not go on with that discussion.
The second point raised by the Prime Minister on that occasion was that it would not be fair to permit extra time for the discussion of that particular public bill brought in by a private member, that all these bills should be treated in the same way, and that no preference should be given to any one. It is quite evident from the resolution before us that for some reason or other the government is anxious that more time should be apportioned to the debate on these particular pipe-line bills than the ordinary rules of the house would permit. I simply want to register my protest on the ground that the particular measure which we were discussing on October 28, namely, the question of federal aid to education, was in my humble opinion of just as great a public interest as is either of the bills before us, and for which special time is being provided in this resolution.
The second point on which I wish to register my protest is the extent, as has already been said, to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) at least, and today the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), are placing the whole weight of the government behind these bills through the introduction of the resolution which is now before us.
When this question was under debate, as is recorded on page 1806 of Hansard-the quotation has already been placed on Hansard- the Minister of Trade and Commerce ended his speech in this way:
I hope that this house will grant the Incorporations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to labour the matter at all, but I do wish to refer to one fact. The course suggested by the motion amounts to a suspension of the rules. Under standing order 116 a suspension of the rule can only take place in cases of "urgent and pressing necessity".
I have no feelings in regard to the pipe line bill that will go to a committee. But when I find a motion such as this with no

Business of the House
explanation as to any pressing emergency or necessity I wonder whether everything is above the surface as it should be. As I look at the situation I would have thought that the Prime Minister-if ever there was a Prime Minister of our country with a knowledge of the law to equal his, I am not aware of the fact-would have laid a foundation, as he led off on this motion, to let the house and the country know what are the matters of "urgent and pressing necessity" that require a complete change in our rules.
Because of the ruling that you made I find myself, sir, in the position of all those who have preceded me, of being unable to discuss this matter as I should like. With the greatest deference I say this. If the onus is on us to show that there is no urgency or pressing necessity for this, the facts of the bill would have to be discussed in order to show it. You, sir, having so ruled, the discussion as a result becomes more or less theoretical. The only justification advanced was by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, which apparently is that a filibuster has taken place. I have looked up the meaning of filibuster. Filibuster means this: any one or a group who attempt to prevent legislation by prolonged speaking to consume time. Obstruction, of course, is to block and to hinder. How many spoke on this matter? I think the total number who have spoken, including the minister, was seven or eight hon. members. The total discussion on this subject amounted to some two and a half hours. But the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with that peculiar affection for parliament and parliamentary procedure that he has always shown, was fearful that parliament was being circumvented.
He gave the House of Commons an hour of grace on November 15. I have read the reports in the British Journals, and I find no case where at any time any minister, much less a prime minister, became an active proponent of a bill introduced by a private member. What is the reason for this solicitude? No one knows. Why the urgency? Would discussion for a few more days have possibly brought other matters to light? The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank) was one who took a firm stand; was he an obstructionist? Was any speech delivered by any member of the house on this matter other than a fair and proper discussion and an examination of matters deserving to be examined by parliament?
What are we coming to? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed out that there were no precedents for this course in Canada. I ask the Prime

Minister when he replies to answer why this rush, why this endeavour to put the matter before a committee and thus deny a legitimate and proper criticism in parliament?
There is more to this than appears upon the surface. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) gave the house an hour of grace. His words were these-and he wants them quoted:
I should like also to say a word about what seems obviously to be a filibuster in connection with these bills. The government will not permit any small number of members to prevent this house as a whole from voting on a private bill.
Where was this small group of members? Members in all parts of the house spoke, seven in all-

I was discussing it as another example similar to this that occurred within the last few days. In this case parliament refused to follow the direction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It did not dance to his dictatorial tune. In effect he ordered the house on November 15 in these words, "you have a few more days, and then this government will see to it that your rights shall be denied."
Sir, this morning the Prime Minister spoke with almost contemptuous disregard of the rights of minorities in parliament. We have a government with an overwhelming majority, supported as it must be by its membership-

for, after all, every government has power over the membership following it to insist upon obedience.
Is there any member supporting the government who dare stand in the House of Commons and show his independence after the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have thrown themselves wholeheartedly behind this motion? Quintin Hogg in his book on parliament says:
The rights of minorities and individuals are as indispensable a factor in a democracy as the privileges of an anonymous majority.
I say again that if there was any suggestion of filibustering, then the Prime Minister has his rights in order to prevent such filibustering. He has his rights under the rules. But instead of exercising the rights he possesses under the rules, he decides to change the rules. If there was filibustering the Prime Minister had power to apply closure, as it has been applied in proper cases. Instead of doing that he adopts the backdoor method of introducing an amendment to change the rules for the occasion. Parliamentary rules have stood the test in this country for eighty years, and in the mother of parliaments for two hundred years. It is dangerous to parliamentary government when rules become a monopoly of the Prime Minister and the government to be changed whenever they deem it necessary.
The motion in its present form mutilates parliamentary procedure, and I use those words advisedly. For it places in the hands of the government of this country, supported as it is by an overwhelming majority, the right at any time, at the wish and whim of the Minister of Trade and Commerce-and, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), so often says, I say this in a spirit of kindliness-

speechtext: "In a kindly way"-get it right.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSIDERATION OF PRIVATE BILLS

-to circumvent parliament and parliamentary procedure.
Nothing can stop the government from doing what it will with the rules for it is omnipotent. It is omnipotent because of its overwhelming majority. It is omnipotent because of the control the cabinet has over its followers, in that there are two sanctions that can be applied against independence, one being the threat of dissolution and the other the threat of preferment.
I have not spoken on these pipe line bills. The opposition has a right to demand the preservation of the rules of parliament, and not to have them changed at the will of the government. Parliamentary rules are designed to deny the short-cuts in parliamentary procedure which have taken place on a number of recent occasions.
Business of the House
In my opinion the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) does not meet the situation. Proper debate is not filibuster. Indeed, in an important matter that was before parliament some weeks ago, the question of grants for education to the provinces, was talked out by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). He spoke on it, no vote, the debate was adjourned, and private members' days were ended. There was no question of a filibuster by the Prime Minister, but that was the effect of what occurred.
I am not interested either directly or indirectly in any of these applicant companies. I have no views with regard to them although I have heard arguments on both sides. I am concerned with this motion which transcends the fortunes of any company, whether any of the principals in that company were interested in Beauharnois or not. This motion is but another example of an arbitrary attitude of mind on the part of this government. The government seems to develop that arbitrary turn of mind from being led or misled by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Throughout the years this attitude has revealed itself, in this case in interference with the rules of parliament and in other cases by circumvention of parliamentary tradition and procedure.
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, many hon. gentlemen have spoken of the government's overwhelming majority, and the hon. gentleman who has just sat down has referred to the many occasions when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had circumvented parliament. I can assure hon. members that if the government has an overwhelming majority it is because of the opinion of the people of Canada about the Minister of Trade and Commerce. On every occasion and on every platform where I appeared during the campaign I never failed to pay tribute to the great service that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had rendered to this country and to assert that although the path might not be easy for trade in the months or years to come there was no man in Canada better fitted to guide Canadian trade during that period than the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The response that was made was such that it enables hon. gentlemen who have spoken in this debate to jeer at the fact that the government has an overwhelming majority. They forget that that overwhelming majority was sent here by the electors of this nation.
